subject: Cloud Computing
title: Dropbox and the Storage Revolution
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Dropbox and the Storage Revolution.

hook.text: Drew Houston forgot his USB drive on a bus. He built Dropbox so nobody would need one again.

buildup.text: Dropbox stored your files in the cloud and synced them across every device automatically.

discovery.text: It launched in 2008 and reached 100 million users in five years with almost no advertising.

twist.text: Dropbox ran on AWS for years, then moved to its own servers to save $75 million over two years.

climax.text: A cloud storage company left the cloud because it got too expensive at massive scale.

punchline.text: The cloud isn't always cheapest. Dropbox did the math.

quiz.question: Why did Dropbox eventually move off AWS?
options: Running its own servers saved tens of millions of dollars at its scale
AWS refused to continue hosting Dropbox
Dropbox wanted to switch to Google Cloud instead

details.summary: Dropbox launched in 2008 and popularized cloud storage by making file syncing effortless. It initially ran entirely on AWS before building its own infrastructure. Dropbox proved that consumers would trust personal files to the cloud if the experience was seamless enough.
details.whyItMatters: Dropbox made cloud storage mainstream for consumers. Its later migration off AWS also showed that cloud is not always the final destination for every workload.
takeaways: Dropbox made cloud file syncing simple and mainstream
It initially ran on AWS then built its own infrastructure
Consumer trust in cloud storage grew through simple experiences

faq.question: Why did Dropbox leave AWS?
faq.answer: At Dropbox's scale, the cost of storing exabytes of data on S3 exceeded the cost of building and operating their own storage infrastructure. By building custom hardware in colocation facilities, Dropbox saved tens of millions of dollars annually while maintaining performance.

faq.question: What is cloud repatriation?
faq.answer: Cloud repatriation is moving workloads from public cloud back to owned infrastructure. At very high scale, the economics of public cloud can become unfavorable. Dropbox, Basecamp, and others have repatriated specific workloads, though most organizations still find cloud more cost-effective.
